title: Exercise 2 — k-NN as an object, metrics, splitting, standardization
text:
What you will learn

How the number of neighbours \(k\) changes a prediction, and why \(k = 1\) is a noisy vote — first at the blackboard, then in code.
How to write a model as a class with fit and predict, and check it against scikit-learn.
How to compute accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, precision, \(F_1\) and balanced accuracy by hand from a confusion matrix, and how to check accuracy, the sensitivity/specificity pair and the two regression errors MSE and MAE, written in NumPy, against sklearn.metrics.
Why a model is measured on data it has never seen, and how much a single hold-out split moves.
Why k-NN needs feature scaling — the z-score and min–max normalization — and how to recognise four classic ways of reporting a number that is too good to be true.

Task 3a — the metrics. A classifier decides for each of 100 leaves whether it is a maple (the positive class); 20 of them really are maples. Its confusion matrix — rows are the actual class, columns the prediction, as in the lecture — is:

Compute, as exact fractions and then as decimals:

accuracy \(= (TP + TN) / (TP + TN + FP + FN)\)
sensitivity (recall) \(= TP / (TP + FN)\)
specificity \(= TN / (TN + FP)\)
precision \(= TP / (TP + FP)\)
\(F_1 = 2 \cdot \dfrac{\text{precision} \cdot \text{recall}}{\text{precision} + \text{recall}} = 2\,TP / (2\,TP + FP + FN)\)
balanced accuracy \(=\) the mean of the per-class recalls \(= \frac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{TP}{TP + FN} + \dfrac{TN}{TN + FP}\right)\) — also for the two constant classifiers “always maple” and “always not maple”

Then answer in one sentence: the accuracy looks good, so why would you not want to report only that number?

PCA formulas (optional reference)
Let \(X\in\mathbb R^{n\times d}\) contain samples in rows and features in columns. The steps follow the third lecture:

Centre each feature: \(\bar x_j=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n X_{ij}\), \((X_c)_{ij}=X_{ij}-\bar x_j\).
Covariance: \(S=\frac1n X_c^\top X_c\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}\).
Principal directions: \(S\mathbf w_j=\lambda_j\mathbf w_j\), \(\|\mathbf w_j\|_2=1\). Keep the directions with the largest eigenvalues.
Projection: \(W_k=[\mathbf w_1,\ldots,\mathbf w_k]\), \(Z=X_cW_k\in\mathbb R^{n\times k}\). For one component, \(\mathbf z=X_c\mathbf w_1\).
Variance retained: \(r_k=\dfrac{\lambda_1+\cdots+\lambda_k}
{\lambda_1+\cdots+\lambda_d}\), with \(\lambda_1\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_d\).

section: 1. Recap: from the basics to the habits
text:
1. Recap: from the basics to the habits
The fifth lecture in one page, in the same order. Read it before the lab and keep it open while you work; the terms used in the tasks are defined here.

What a language model does

A language model continues text: given everything so far, it estimates how likely each next piece is, picks one, appends it, repeats. The result is plausible text, not checked truth. (The network behind it is a transformer, eleventh lecture.)
Token = a piece of text: a word, part of a word, a number, punctuation. Your message, the reply, every file and every error the agent reads are counted in tokens.
Context window = how many tokens the model can read at once.
It learned once. Training (read a lot of text and code → learn from examples of good answers → get rewarded for better ones) changed the model before you used it. A correction in the chat is only read in this session. In a new session it is gone, unless you write it into a file.



Chatbot vs. agent









Chatbot
Agent




You ask for a plot of data.csv
It writes plotting code as text
It reads the CSV, writes the code, runs it and fixes the error


Who runs, checks and fixes
You: copy, run, paste the error back
The agent; you check the result


What it can reach
Only what you paste into the chat
Your project files, the terminal, a browser, a server


What you get
An answer
Files: plot.py, plot.html, and evidence that they work




Model = the trained network that writes text. Agent = a model plus software that can act.
Harness = the program you install (Claude Code, Codex). It sends your request to the model and carries out the actions the model asks for. Agent = model + harness + tools: the model decides, the harness does it. The model never touches your files itself.
Tool = an action the harness does for the model: read a file, edit a file, run a command (python, git, ssh), open a browser. A tool returns evidence: file contents, an error message, a screenshot.
Terminal = a text window: you type a command, a program runs, text comes back. The agent uses it the same way, so anything you can start by typing, the agent can use.
The loop. One turn: the model proposes an action → the harness runs it → the result goes back to the model. A task takes many turns. Example, plot measurements.csv: read the first lines to learn the column names → write plot.py and run it → KeyError: 'temperature' (the column is temperature_C) → fix the script, run it again, open the plot → hand over plot.html and say what was checked. An error is information, not failure. The loop stops when the goal is done, it needs your permission, or information is missing. The same error repeated without investigating is your cue to step in.
Context = everything the model reads before this answer: your request, the rules file, the files it has read, the tool outputs. Like a desk: only what lies on the desk counts, not the files in the cabinet (your disk). A file is on the desk only after a tool has read it.



Your first session: where it runs, how much it may do, who pays
Every setup is four separate choices. Today’s answers:








Layer
Question
Today




Model
Who thinks?
Qwen 3.8 Flash, behind CERIT-SC’s alias agentic (not Claude)


Provider
Who runs it and bills you?
CERIT-SC (e-INFRA CZ), free for students


Harness
Which program do you talk to?
Claude Code


Your computer
Where do the commands run?
Your laptop; in the class-server task of part 4 the agent also sends commands to another computer over SSH




Provider = the service that runs the model. Endpoint = its web address. API key = your personal password for programs. Keep the key out of chats, screenshots and Git.
Which program. Claude Code (Anthropic, used today), Codex (OpenAI: terminal, VS Code extension and desktop app), Antigravity CLI (Google, successor of Gemini CLI for individuals), Copilot CLI (GitHub), OpenCode (open source, connects almost any model, even a local one). Codex and Claude Code are currently probably the strongest. OpenClaw and Hermes Agent are harnesses for an always-on personal assistant, not for coding sessions.
Where to type. The terminal (cd my-project, then claude) is recommended: it combines naturally with Python, Git and SSH. The same agent also lives in a VS Code extension (files, code, agent and its changes in one window) and a desktop app (several tasks side by side).
Permission modes. The agent wants to run pip install pandas. Who says yes?







Mode
What happens




Plan
It only reads and proposes; nothing changes.


Ask (default)
It asks, you press yes or no.


Accept edits (acceptEdits)
File edits go through; commands still ask.


Auto (recommended)
An automatic check decides the routine requests. With CERIT-SC it is slow and often blocks; then use Accept edits.


Bypass
It just runs, with no check. Only on a separate, throwaway machine.



Shift+Tab cycles the modes; Esc interrupts the agent.
Who pays. A subscription (ChatGPT Plus or Claude Pro, $20/month; higher tiers raise the limits) includes agent use within limits. An API key is billed per token, separately; a chat plan is not API credit. Every turn resends the whole conversation, so the input adds up: five turns of 10k–30k tokens are 100,000 input tokens for one small task; with 20,000 output tokens that is ≈ $0.80 on Claude Opus 5.5, $2 on GPT-6 Astra, but only ≈ $0.05–0.21 on the cheap Chinese DeepSeek and Kimi models (prices of 30 September and 2 October 2026; their servers are in China, so no personal data). For heavy agent use the API can cost much more than a subscription; light use can be cheaper. Today: CERIT-SC, free.
A model on your own computer. Open-weight models (e.g. via Ollama) keep the data at home and have no meter, but need memory (parameters × bits ÷ 8: a 70 B model at 4 bits needs 35 GB just for the weights) and are weaker at long tool chains. Agent on your laptop ≠ model on your laptop: Claude Code on your laptop still sends your files to a hosted model.
A server that stays on. SSH = log in to another computer’s terminal. tmux keeps a terminal session alive on the server: start the agent in tmux, detach (Ctrl-b, then d), close the laptop, later tmux attach brings the same terminal back. Remote control (Claude Code, Codex) lets you check a session from your phone; it needs the provider’s account, not CERIT-SC.



Goal and context

Ask for the result, not the steps: “one HTML file with the row count, missing values and class balance of data.csv; do not change the CSV; open the result in a browser” instead of “make a nice report”.
Goal · Context · Constraints · Done when. The four parts of a good task. A missing “done when” is the most common reason an agent stops too early or claims success without evidence. In part 5 you write these four headings yourself in SPEC.md.
What goes into context: file paths, the exact error and the command that caused it, a screenshot of the wrong plot, an example of the output you want. Ask it to read the file, not guess.
Three files. AGENTS.md = the rules, read at every start (Claude Code reads CLAUDE.md; the line @AGENTS.md in it loads the shared file). SPEC.md = the task. PLAN.md = where we stopped: what is done, what was checked, the next step. All in Markdown (plain text with # headings and - bullets).
Long is not better. A crowded context makes the model worse: it forgets decisions, repeats a fixed error. Save the state into PLAN.md, /clear, then “Read SPEC.md and PLAN.md, look at what changed, continue with the first unfinished step.” /compact summarises instead, but details can be lost.
Subagent = a helper the agent starts for a side task (a search, a long log, a review) with its own fresh context; it returns only a short summary. It keeps your context clean and gives a fresh pair of eyes; it costs tokens and does not see your chat, so the brief must stand alone.
Steering: “Stop. Explain the cause and try a different approach.” · “Return to the agreed scope. Show me what you changed.” · “Run the check and show the output.” · “Read this file, then revise the plan.” · “I cannot” is a hypothesis: “Look for a tool or a command, try a small example, and tell me the real blocker.”



Check the result

Give it eyes. A browser it can drive (Playwright), a rendered image, a test it can run. Writing the HTML is only the first step; “Open the page, try the filter and inspect a screenshot. Fix what you find.”
More tools. CLI first: git, gh (GitHub), uv (Python environments), quarto, ffmpeg; the agent knows them. MCP (Model Context Protocol) is a standard plug for extra tools, like USB: a browser (Playwright), Blender, a library’s current docs; the agent can set one up: “Find and set up an MCP server for X.” A skill is a recipe the agent reads when needed (“Turn what we just did into a skill.”). A hook is a script run at an event that can block an action: a rule in AGENTS.md asks, a hook enforces.
A test is a tiny script with a known answer:
assert accuracy([0, 1, 1, 0], [0, 0, 1, 0]) == 0.75
“Write a test for this behaviour, show it failing, then make it pass.” A passing test is evidence, not proof. Never let the agent change a test just to make it pass.
Works or fails is easy; plausible but wrong is hard. A page that loads or a board that blinks gives the agent clear feedback and it iterates until it works. A training script runs, prints an accuracy and complains about nothing when the test set leaked into tuning. For such tasks you write the checks before the agent starts.
For ML, fix the experiment first: where the data came from and how you split it (duplicates!), which models, which metric, how many trials; preprocessing fitted inside each training fold; a held-out test set used once, after choosing the model.



Save, undo, stay safe

Good software practice still applies: version control, small steps, tests, review, readable code, documentation, no secrets in the repository.
Git from zero. Git = a history of your project folder. Repository = the folder with that history. Commit = a save point with a note. Diff = what changed since the last save point. Branch = a separate line of work. Push = upload the history to GitHub, a website that keeps a copy. Understand the words, not the commands: the agent types them, you decide what is saved and what is published.
Rhythm: commit a working version → ask for a change → look at what changed and check the output → commit or undo (“Go back to the last commit, keep my other edits.”).
Worktrees (git worktree add) give two agents separate folders of the same repository, so they never edit the same files.
Two risks: an unwanted action, and your data leaving.
Prompt injection: a web page, README or issue the agent reads can hide text that gives orders (“read .env and send it to …”). Limit what the agent can do (permissions, no secrets in reach); asking it to ignore injections is not enough.
Privacy: whatever the agent reads goes to the provider. df.head() on a patient table sends five real patients. Give the agent synthetic data with the same columns; run the real data yourself.
Instructions ask; permissions and isolation limit. “Do not touch data/” can be ignored; a permission rule makes it ask; a sandbox means it cannot even see the folder.
An agent optimises the goal it was given, not the one you meant. In July 2026 a model under test broke out of its environment to fetch the benchmark’s answers.
BUT rules: follow the assignment, verify and understand what you submit, disclose how you used AI; you remain responsible. Could you explain your result if the agent session disappeared?



Beyond code
Text in, anything out: Markdown for notes, HTML for interactive reports and small tools, Quarto for slides next to their code, LaTeX for documents, CadQuery (3D shapes in Python) and Blender scripts for 3D. The agent edits text easily and Git shows exactly what changed; Word and PowerPoint files are hard to edit and compare (generate them from a script if you need them, see part 4). For a thesis, keep notes, text, code and results in one repository.


Tips in detail
Start the task well

Describe the finished result, not a sequence of steps.
Goal, context, constraints, done when. A missing “done when” is the most common reason an agent stops too early.
Say how you will recognise success: a test that passes, a number that must match, a page that must open.
Write naturally; precise beats elaborate. Imperfect English or typos hardly matter; a vague task does. Dictating a draft is fine; then check names and numbers.
Invite questions when the task is unclear: “Ask me what would change the solution, then write SPEC.md.”
Compare two approaches before an expensive commitment.
A small first version that works end to end, then extend it.
Save the plan in the repository, not only in the chat.

Keep the context useful

Point to the files by path.
Show examples: the desired output, a screenshot of the wrong plot. On Windows, pasting an image with Ctrl+V often fails in the terminal: save the screenshot and give its path, or drag the file in.
Ask it to read the source before it guesses.
Give the exact error and the command that caused it, not “it fails”.
Excerpts, not dumps: the relevant lines, not a whole dataset or log.
Give it the sources: the PDFs, data and papers, or let it download them. Have PDFs converted to Markdown; ask it to search the web for current documentation.
One source of rules: AGENTS.md for rules, SPEC.md for the task, PLAN.md for where you stopped.
Have everything written into files, immediately: a correction in the chat is forgotten in the next session. A repeated mistake becomes a rule in AGENTS.md.
/clear often, not only when it drifts: save the state, /clear, then “Read SPEC.md and PLAN.md, look at what changed, continue with the first unfinished step.”

Steer the work

Try Auto; if it keeps blocking, use Accept edits. Never Bypass to escape prompts.
One project folder, with a subfolder per task.
Commit before a substantial change and look at what changed after it.
Interrupt early with Esc when it goes the wrong way.
Same failure repeated? “Stop. Explain the cause and try a different approach.”
Unrelated edits? “Return to the agreed scope. Show me what you changed.”
A claim without evidence? “Run the check and show the output.”
“I cannot”? Find out which it is: no tool, no access, or no idea.

Check the result

Run it yourself with real inputs and an edge case.
Look at it: open the page, the figure, the PDF, the 3D model. A program that finished without error can still draw the wrong plot.
Check where the files landed; a model may report success with files written somewhere else.
Ask for files and evidence, not a promise that it is done.
A fresh reviewer: “Start a subagent that reviews the diff against SPEC.md. It should find bugs, not praise.” (if your setup supports subagents; otherwise a new session with the same request) The agent that wrote the code nearly always approves it. Another model (/model thinker) helps further.
Ask it to simplify: first versions are verbose. Every so often let it refactor thoroughly, with the tests passing before and after.
For ML, freeze the test data before tuning; choose the model without it.

Make durable outputs

Markdown for notes, HTML for interactive reports and small tools, Quarto for slides next to their code, LaTeX for documents.
Keep the source, not only the output: the script that made the figure, the parameters of the 3D model.
Record the model and date you used in RUNS.md.
Compare costs per checked result, not per token: a stronger model with fewer retries can be cheaper.

Work through the examples with the teacher: ask for a result, look at it, then ask for a change. Complete at least three of the tasks below yourself. TipEasy · A game: Snake with a twist

Goal: find out how well the tree type can be predicted from leaf height and width — with a number you can trust. Try several classical classifiers from the lectures, tune their hyperparameters, compare them fairly, and present the result in an HTML report and a five-slide Quarto presentation.

Writing the assignment for the agent is your job. There is no prepared prompt. The evaluation design is yours, from the second lecture; the agent can help you think it through, but you decide.

1. One neuron by hand
The laptop stays closed. One neuron with two inputs, no bias, and the squared-error loss \(L = \tfrac12 (\hat y - y)^2\):

Compute the inner potential \(a = w_1 x_1 + w_2 x_2\).
For the linear activation \(f(a) = a\): the prediction \(\hat y\), the loss \(L\) and the gradient \(\nabla_{\mathbf w} L = (\hat y - y)\, f'(a)\, \mathbf x\).
The same for the sigmoid, \(f'(a) = f(a)\big(1 - f(a)\big)\).
One step \(\mathbf w \leftarrow \mathbf w - \eta \nabla_{\mathbf w} L\) of the sigmoid neuron, then the new \(a\), \(\hat y\) and \(L\) — did the loss go down?

Why is the sigmoid gradient eight times smaller than the linear one, although the input, the target and the loss function are the same? Then write the same formulas in NumPy and reproduce your paper.


2. One neuron in NumPy
A linear neuron with one input is linear regression. Write the whole SGD loop — epochs, reshuffling, per-sample update, the loss curve — on 100 noisy samples of \(y = 0.5x + 2\). Compare the result with np.linalg.lstsq, and explain why SGD with a constant learning rate only gets close. Then compute the gradient both analytically and by a central difference.


3. A two-layer network
ReLU hidden layer, linear output, one sample per column. Write the network as one plain script, line by line: first the forward pass, the loss and the backward pass for one mini-batch, then the same lines in a training loop with the update. The supplied gradient check compares your backward pass with finite differences on every parameter before you train with it.
This is the slide “General neural net — each layer and NN learning” of the lecture, with the bias written as a separate vector \(\mathbf b_k\) and the loss averaged over a mini-batch of \(n\) samples (one sample per column of \(\mathbf h_0\)):



Layer \(k\): inputs \(\mathbf h_{k-1}\), inner potentials \(\mathbf a_k\), outputs \(\mathbf h_k\) (in the figure, \(m\) counts the inputs and \(n\) the neurons of the layer; below, \(n\) is the number of samples in a mini-batch).


Forward, from the first layer to the last, with \(\mathbf h_0 = \mathbf x\) and \(\hat{\mathbf y} = \mathbf h_K\): \[\mathbf a_k = W_k \mathbf h_{k-1} + \mathbf b_k\] \[\mathbf h_k = f(\mathbf a_k)\]
Backward, from the last layer to the first, starting with \(\nabla_{\hat{\mathbf y}} L = (\hat{\mathbf y} - \mathbf y)/n\): \[\nabla_{\mathbf a_k} L = \nabla_{\mathbf h_k} L \odot f'(\mathbf a_k)\] \[\nabla_{W_k} L = \nabla_{\mathbf a_k} L \; \mathbf h_{k-1}^T\] \[\nabla_{\mathbf b_k} L = \textstyle\sum_{\text{batch}} \nabla_{\mathbf a_k} L\] \[\nabla_{\mathbf h_{k-1}} L = W_k^T \nabla_{\mathbf a_k} L\]
Update every layer: \(W_k \leftarrow W_k - \eta \nabla_{W_k} L\), the same for \(\mathbf b_k\).
Here \(K = 2\), \(f\) is ReLU in the hidden layer and the identity at the output (\(f' = 1\)). Every gradient has the shape of what it differentiates: \(\nabla_{W_k} L\) is as large as \(W_k\) — the quickest check of your code.


4. Any number of layers
Your script as functions, with the recipe above and \(K\) as a variable: the weights and biases in Python lists W[k], b[k], the forward pass as a loop from the first layer to the last, the backward pass as a loop from the last to the first. A skeleton with the lists and the loops is given; you fill in the body of each loop. With the layer sizes [1, 128, 1] it must reproduce your Task 3 loss curve exactly; a gradient check on a tiny network with two hidden layers follows, and then you train a deeper network on the same data.


5. From your code to PyTorch
The same lists and loops, with tensors. Replace one piece at a time: first autograd (loss.backward()) instead of your backward pass, then torch.optim.SGD instead of your update. The loss curve stays the same throughout. The training loop is given; you write only the lines that change. A short tour with runnable examples comes first: tensors, NumPy conversion, a gradient with backward() and its accumulation, no_grad(), detach() and the device.


6. Your network on blood-cell images, with an agent
↓ Download everything for the final task (ZIP)
Includes the student notebook, the task with its requirements (TASK.md) and a getting-started README. After extracting, replace the bundled blank notebook with your own notebook before starting the agent.
The practical problem. A blood count with a differential tells a physician how many cells of each type are in the blood. Analysers photograph single cells from a blood smear, and a technician still checks many of them. A classifier that pre-sorts the cells, so that only the uncertain ones need a human, saves real work.
Your extension. The agent starts from your own Task 4 functions — already a loop over any number of ReLU layers — and extends them with a softmax output and the cross-entropy loss, in NumPy only, keeping your conventions (one sample per column, the lists W[k], b[k], the backward formulas of the lecture). The result must pass a finite-difference gradient test on a tiny network, compare a softmax baseline with several network sizes on the validation split, and open the test split only once, at the end. The notebook shows a preview of the data and gives the goal, the graded requirements (each with how you check it in REVIEW.md) and the required files — not a ready-made prompt: writing the instructions for your agent is your job.
Optional editor: if you want to use VS Code on Windows, install it from PowerShell or Windows Terminal:
winget install --id Microsoft.VisualStudioCode --exact --scope user --accept-package-agreements --accept-source-agreements
Start in class: the repository, the invitation, your first instructions, the gradient test and a short trial run. Finish the full run and the review at home.

Theoretical tests are taken in the e-learning: 5 questions, 1 point each, one question per page without going back, 8 minutes, no materials. An answer that mixes correct and incorrect options gets zero points; a partially correct selection gets a proportional part of the point. You may ask for an explanation of a question during the test. Retakes are not possible.


Credit requirements

attendance in the computer labs (see Attendance),
at least 15 points from the semester,
coming to the labs with knowledge of the topics already covered in the lectures.



Final exam — 70 points, at least 35 to pass
Oral exam of 20–30 minutes with two examiners. The topics are split into two areas; you draw one question from each area and each examiner grades one of them. The final score is the average of the two, but a substantial lack of knowledge in either area means zero points for the whole exam. You do not have to memorise equations, but you must be able to explain and interpret every equation on the slides. The exam can be taken in Czech or English. Erasmus students who cannot register for a full date should e-mail the guarantor.
The list of topics from the last exam is on the materials page; the 2026/27 list is published before the exam period.

title: Organisation
text:
Attendance

Computer labs are compulsory. At most two excused absences are allowed for the semester.
A missed lab cannot normally be made up at another time. Work through the notebook on your own; the tests assume the material of every lab.
Prolonged absence for serious reasons is dealt with individually: contact the lab teacher or the guarantor as soon as you know about it and a form of compensation will be agreed.

title: Organisation
text:
Rules for using AI

Labs 1–4: switch the AI assistance in Colab off (Settings → AI assistance). You write the code yourself, because the point of these labs is to understand what the algorithm does — including when the code is later written by an agent.
Labs 5–12: a coding agent is part of the work; the setup is done in lab 5. Git is mandatory from lab 5 on.
Tests: no AI tools and no materials during the theoretical tests. The practical tests are about understanding and checking code, which is exactly what you have to do with an agent’s output anyway.
Project: you may use any tool; the result is what is graded. Be able to explain every line you submit.

One credit corresponds to 26 hours of work, so five credits are roughly two hours of lectures, three hours of lab and about four hours of your own preparation per week, plus the preparation for the exam (directive on credits).
